title: Why Rules And Consequences Aren't Enough https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2013/02/02/why-rules-and-consequences-arent-enough/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that rules and consequences alone cannot control a classroom unless students genuinely want to be part of it. Prompted by teacher emails about excessive time-outs, he revisits the core principle that a management plan only works if students have something to lose by being removed from class. He identifies three broad categories teachers must strengthen to create that leverage: relationships, routines, and lessons. Without them, applying consequences to an already unmotivated class will backfire, causing behavior to worsen rather than improve. The piece frames the teacher's job as building enough goodwill and structure that students see time-out as a real loss, not an escape. He closes by insisting this approach works for any teacher, in any setting, 100% of the time.
points: A classroom management plan only works when students have genuine reasons to want to be part of the classroom.
Applying consequences to an unmotivated class without first building buy-in makes behavior worse, not better.
Effective classroom culture rests on three pillars: relationships, routines, and engaging lessons.
The wider the gap between the privilege of class membership and the misery of time-out, the fewer behavior problems arise.
Building this kind of classroom is achievable for any teacher regardless of school, students, or experience level.
quotes: If sitting in time-out doesn’t remove your students from something they want to be part of, then it isn’t a consequence.
Typically, greater than half of most classrooms, and sometimes every student, need something more. They need a reason to listen and learn and care about sitting in your classroom.
The relationship you have with your students is the most important factor in gaining the leverage you need to create the well-behaved class you want.
Routines are about students knowing what you expect of them throughout every minute of the school day.

Searching out rules and consequences and then abruptly applying them to an already unruly classroom will cause behavior to get worse—because unhappy, unmotivated students will resent and rebel against your efforts to control their only source of stimulation.
There must be a distinct and ever-widening gulf between the special feeling they have being a valued member of your class, and the remorse they feel sitting alone and apart in time-out.
